paper.title: Conformal Risk Control
paper.page_convention: 1-based PDF page numbers; PDF p.N equals the rendered page image assets/pages/page-NNN.png

claims.claim: CRC chooses a post-processing parameter lambda from a calibration split to control the expected test loss of a monotone bounded loss function.

evidence.note: Risk definition and lambda selection rule are stated before the main theorem.
Supplementary implementation computes empirical risk with the finite-sample correction.

caveats: The base model and loss must already be defined; CRC is a calibration protocol, not a classifier.

claims.claim: The finite-sample guarantee requires exchangeable random loss functions that are non-increasing in lambda, right-continuous, bounded, and able to reach the target risk at lambda_max.

evidence.note: The theorem lists the assumptions and concludes E[L_{n+1}(lambda_hat)] <= alpha.

caveats: The guarantee is marginal over the random calibration/test draw, not conditional per individual point.

claims.claim: For continuous i.i.d. losses, the procedure is tight up to a 2B/(n+1) lower-bound gap, but this does not make it a high-probability calibration guarantee.

evidence.note: The lower bound and tightness example quantify conservativeness.
Appendix comparison contrasts expectation CRC with RCPS/LTT high-probability procedures.

caveats: The tightness statement relies on extra continuity/i.i.d. assumptions.

claims.claim: The experiments show CRC can control task-specific monotone risks across segmentation, multilabel classification, hierarchical classification, and QA examples.

evidence.note: Risk histograms are centered near the specified alpha values across 1000 random data splits.
The paper reports mean and standard deviation for risk in each worked example.

caveats: These are worked examples, not exhaustive stress tests for arbitrary deployments.

claims.claim: CRC differs from RCPS/LTT by giving an expectation guarantee with a simpler and more sample-efficient monotone-risk procedure, while RCPS/LTT offer high-probability risk bounds.

evidence.note: The paper lists conceptual differences and reports the polyp comparison.
Figure 5 compares FNR and time over n.

caveats: The empirical comparison is on the polyp dataset and selected baselines, not all risk-control methods.

claims.claim: CRC strictly generalizes split conformal prediction: miscoverage is one special binary loss, while CRC targets general expected monotone losses.

evidence.note: The paper shows miscoverage and expected loss side by side.
The appendix states the reduction from conformal prediction to risk control.

caveats: CRC does not automatically produce classical set coverage semantics unless the loss is miscoverage.

claims.claim: Standard CRC does not automatically survive distribution shift; the paper gives weighted and total-variation extensions that require information about the shift.

evidence.note: Distribution shift extension uses likelihood ratios or total variation terms.
Synthetic covariate-shift experiment shows standard CRC fails while covariate-shift correction controls risk.

caveats: Arbitrary campaign/platform/time shifts without validated weights or exchangeability are outside the finite-sample guarantee.

claims.claim: For CogGuard selective Harmfulness, CRC can calibrate thresholds, prediction sets, or abstention policies against a pre-defined harm loss, but it cannot create Gold labels, define harmfulness, or solve OOD shift by itself.

evidence.note: The protocol assumes a loss and calibration data are already available.
The assumptions imply a same-population/exchangeability requirement for the calibration and test losses.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1 and Figure 6, PDF p.8 and p.16
evidence.note: Shift requires an explicit correction, not automatic validity.

caveats: This is a transfer inference from the paper's formal guarantees, not an experiment in harmfulness detection.

limitations: Loss must be monotone or deliberately monotonized; non-monotone losses have no finite-sample guarantee in the basic algorithm.
Exchangeability is central; arbitrary distribution shift needs additional assumptions or weighted extensions.
Guarantee is in expectation, not high probability over every calibration sample or subgroup.
Experiments are illustrative worked examples across CV and NLP, not a harmfulness-classification benchmark.

Supplementary ZIP was preserved completely, but full extraction of long output paths was not completed due to Windows path limitations; selected README and core implementation files were extracted for inspection.
